​Donald Trump issued an executive order requiring U.S. federal agencies to replace the term "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) with "Super Intelligence" (SI) in official communications. 

​Why the Name Change?

​"Artificial" Sounds "Fake": Trump stated that using "artificial" makes the technology sound fake or synthetic when it is actually real and "amazing".

​Bigger Than the Internet: He argued that "Super Intelligence" more accurately reflects a breakthrough far larger than the internet or the Industrial Revolution.

​Rebrand vs. The Real Threat

​While renaming technology shifts the political focus toward power and economic dominance, tech experts argue that debating terminology is a distraction from the real issue: safety and oversight.

​Industry pioneers and tech leaders—including Bill Gates, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei (Anthropic), and Sam Altman (OpenAI)—have repeatedly warned of profound risks, including cybersecurity vulnerabilities, biosecurity threats, and the existential danger of losing human control over super-capable autonomous systems. Many have urged a slower, more deliberate pace of development to ensure systems are properly aligned before they scale further. 

​Rebranding AI to "Super Intelligence" acknowledges its potential, but changing the name does not solve the safety, governance, and control challenges that lie ahead.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

This week, 119 nations gathered in Abu Dhabi and adopted the Abu Dhabi Declaration a five-year global roadmap for crime prevention and criminal justice. Adopted by acclamation. More than 40 ministers of justice in the room. The largest gathering of criminal justice policymakers on earth.

Abu Dhabi. The United Arab Emirates.

The same UAE where Golden Global Bank was designated for converting Iranian oil revenues to cash and gold for the Revolutionary Guard. The same UAE where Spain dismantled the Banca de Dubái a $2 billion crypto narcobank routing European cocaine money. The same UAE where Saudi Arabia's central bank secretly flagged bank transfers as high-risk. The same UAE that extradited Daniel Kinahan one of Europe's most wanted drug lords. The same UAE that arrested a Swedish money laundering fugitive linked to contract killings and handed evidence to INTERPOL.

That country just hosted 119 nations agreeing on how to fight crime for the next five years.

Here's what they committed to.

The Declaration has four pillars: prevention and resilience, justice and the rule of law, countering evolving crime threats, and international cooperation and innovation.

Under those pillars, 119 countries agreed to dismantle scam centers. The same scam centers this framework has been tracking Xinbi, which processed $36 billion. Three weeks later, Turkey is tearing itself apart.

Here's what happened in order.

September 4  Treasury designated Golden Global Bank in Istanbul. The bank was set up to receive Iranian oil revenues from China and convert them to cash and gold for the IRGC. Treasury Secretary Bessent called it "code for you are out of business."

September 16  The Turkish stock market crashed. Regulators discovered suspected share-price manipulation across multiple investment fund companies. Seven companies managing 131 funds with $17 billion in assets were placed into liquidation.

September 18 Turkey's banking regulator quietly revoked the license of Iran's Bank Mellat one of the largest Iranian banks, operating in Turkey for 44 years. No press conference. No announcement. Just a line in the Official Gazette. The same week, Turkey grounded Iran's Mahan Air.

September 26  The deputy chairwoman of Erdogan's ruling party resigned after allegations that she and her husband sold tens of millions of dollars in shares before the stock market crash. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor launched legal proceedings against 76 people connected to the fund scandal. The ruling party's spokesman said: "All those who are involved in irregularities, corruption, abuse or anything that causes harm will be held accountable."

Three weeks. One country. Everything at once.

Iran's 44-year banking pipeline severed. Iran's military airline grounded. $17 billion in corrupt investment funds  liquidated. The ruling party's own deputy chair resigned and under investigation. 76 people facing prosecution.

That's the pattern.

Treasury hits a country from the outside. The country looks at the message. Then the country starts cleaning from the inside not just the thing Treasury targeted, but everything connected to it. Because once you start pulling the thread, everything attached to it comes loose.

The UAE did the same thing. Treasury hit Dubai's banking corridor. The UAE started arresting fugitives, extraditing drug lords, sharing evidence with European police. A brigadier general went on the record saying they'd take action against anyone exploiting their territory.

Now Turkey. Treasury hit one bank. Turkey revoked an entire 44-year banking relationship, grounded an airline, crashed its corrupt fund sector, and started prosecuting members of its own ruling party.

The same pattern is running everywhere.

Russia convicted 60,000 officials in five years and seized $9.5 billion in property.

China is purging a quarter of its governing body. The chairman of their securities regulator convicted of selling access to the stock market. Fifty ministerial-level investigations this year alone.

Saudi Arabia detained 298 officials in a single sweep including senior military and interior ministry officers.

India doubled its enforcement raids. A single betting app case traced $11.3 billion in criminal proceeds.

The United States tripled its counterintelligence arrests and is running the largest sanctions campaign in history.

And now Turkey a NATO ally that spent years playing both sides is cleaning house in three weeks flat.

Each country calls it something different. Turkey calls it market integrity. China calls it party discipline. Russia calls it anti-corruption. Saudi calls it national security. America calls it enforcement.

But they're all doing the same thing. At the same time. In the same direction.

And each one started with a message from the outside that the country answered from the inside.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

text:
Fake FEMA Badges, Fake "Chaplains"

Mario Cesar Dos Santos Jr., 50, of Massachusetts just pleaded guilty in federal court to wire fraud and the fraudulent use of government seals. He ran an outfit called the Chaplain Emergency Management Agency, Inc., or CEMA, which he falsely claimed was a government agency endorsed by FEMA. Neither he nor CEMA had any authorization to use the seals of FEMA, the Department of Homeland Security, or the FBI, and neither one is affiliated with any federal agency at all.

According to court documents, Dos Santos organized chaplaincy training courses in Florida and other states, and even abroad. The courses were free to attend, but he charged attendees about $400 to $450 to receive a chaplaincy certificate. After they paid, he handed them ID cards, law enforcement badges, and certificates bearing the seals of federal agencies. He told them the badges authorized them to support law enforcement during emergency situations and even take control of emergency situations until police arrived. He also told them their status as CEMA chaplains would give them immunity from immigration enforcement and keep them safe from deportation. Every word of it was false.

The details are brazen. The ID cards carried a doctored DHS seal modified to read "U.S. Department of Homeland Chaplain." The certificates bore the FBI seal. CEMA's website and social media falsely presented it as a federal agency, and even falsely claimed accreditation from real education organizations. Dos Santos sold polo shirts, bumper stickers, jackets, badges, and badge holders with DHS or FEMA seals on them. An undercover operation at a training on September 27, 2025 caught him in the act, and his CEMA group chat had more than 750 members when the investigation began in August 2025. He was arrested February 19, 2026 at Orlando International Airport, where he showed up wearing a CEMA polo shirt with the DHS seal on it.

Here is the part that should make your blood boil. Dos Santos is a Brazilian national who came to the United States in 2016, overstayed his visa, and is now in deportation proceedings. The man selling protection from deportation was an illegal alien himself. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison, with sentencing set for December 18, 2026. The FBI is asking anyone victimized by the scheme to contact CEMAPotentialVictims@fbi.gov by October 30, 2026.

U.S. Attorney Gregory Kehoe said impersonating federal agencies is a serious crime and the missions of these agencies must be protected. The FBI said they will keep investigating fraud schemes that deceive the public and undermine trust in legitimate government agencies.

When the man selling "protection from deportation" is an illegal alien himself, what does that tell you about how broken this system was?

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

What happens when an ordinary Indian is wronged by a powerful tech company?

You appeal to the company that banned you. You explain. You submit documents. You wait. You appeal again.

And if nothing happens, you are told to approach the Government’s Grievance Appellate Committee.

And if that doesn’t help?

Go to court.

But who can actually do that?

Who has the money to hire a lawyer? Who has the time to spend months fighting? Who can afford to keep chasing authorities and corporations just to get back something that was taken away without a fair resolution?

This is the helplessness of the common Indian.

The government has institutions and procedures.

And the ordinary citizen?

They have nowhere to go.

Most people will eventually give up—not because they were wrong, but because they simply cannot afford to keep fighting.

I am fighting my WhatsApp ban. 

But what about the person who doesn’t?

What happens to their rights?

What happens to their livelihood?

What happens to their dignity?

If an ordinary citizen cannot realistically enforce their rights against a powerful corporation, what protection do those rights actually provide?

This is not just about my WhatsApp account.

'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

What if selling a bad insurance policy could cost the salesperson their commission?

That’s what IRDAI has proposed in its latest insurance distribution reforms.

And there’s another interesting part: the person selling the policy could be linked to it. 🧵

But IRDAI is going a step further.

It proposes tagging the functional identity of the salesperson, PoSP, agent or associate to the policy they sell.

In simple terms: the regulator wants to know who sold what.

And if that policy is subsequently established to have been mis-sold, IRDAI has proposed commission clawback.

So the commission earned from a sale may not remain with the distributor if the sale is later found to involve mis-selling.

Inside IRDAI’s Insurance Overhaul: New Rules, a Market Selloff and What It Means for You

On Wednesday, September 23, India’s insurance regulator put out a discussion paper. By Thursday afternoon, one listed company had wiped out more market value in a single session than most Indian unicorns are worth.

What could rattle the entire insurance sector this hard? Not a final rule, a public consultation paper titled “Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution,” open for stakeholder comments until October 25.

Here’s what’s actually in it, why the market reacted the way it did, and why India isn’t the first market to try this.

What Just Happened

IRDAI’s paper — the most significant proposed overhaul of distribution regulation since the 2023 Expenses of Management reforms — touches almost everything: who can sell insurance, how much they can be paid, how insurers account for total distribution spending, and what happens if a policy turns out to have been mis-sold.

The New Three-Tier Structure: IDE, IDP and MII

Today’s distribution architecture runs across roughly eight overlapping categories of intermediaries. IRDAI wants to collapse that into three: Insurance Distribution Entities (IDEs), Insurance Distribution Persons (IDPs) and Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs). In plain terms — an IDE is a company selling insurance, like a bank or broker; an IDP is the individual actually making the sale; and an MII is shared digital infrastructure such as the Bima Sugam platform.

Alongside the new structure, entry capital for distributors would fall sharply to ₹10 lakh, and registration would become permanent rather than something to renew — cheaper to get in, even as per-policy earnings get squeezed.

Why the Caps and the Glide Path Matter

Since 2023, insurers have operated without hard commission caps, working instead within a single entity-level EoM ceiling calculated on gross written premium. The new paper wants to bring back hard, product-specific caps on top of a tighter overall ceiling.

The proposed caps are steep in places: credit life commissions would fall to roughly 2%, against about 28% today; motor own-damage commission would drop to around 5% from 16%; first-year health insurance commission would be capped at 15–20%; and first-year life insurance commission at 20–25%, dropping to 3–5% on renewal.

The overall cost ceiling would also tighten gradually rather than overnight. Life insurers would need to bring EoM down to 15% of premium within two years and 12.5% within five, while general insurers face a glide path from 30% currently to 20% over five years, with the calculation base shifting from gross written premium to the narrower gross direct premium income.

Why Insurance Got This Expensive to Sell

Here’s the structural problem IRDAI is trying to fix. A policy’s headline “base commission” often fails to capture what it actually costs to distribute — promotional expenses, brand fees, rewards and other payments can push what a distributor actually earns 30% to 60% above the base rate. That gap is effectively invisible to the buyer.

IRDAI’s fix is to fold both direct and indirect payments into a single definition of commission, and require insurers and larger distributors to disclose their commission structures in a simple, accessible format.

How to Spot Mis-Selling — and What Changes with the New Seller Registry

This is arguably the most directly useful part of the paper for a reader. IRDAI has proposed documenting customer needs and suitability before a sale, linking the identity of the individual seller to every policy, putting mis-selling information in the public domain, and allowing insurers to claw back commission where mis-selling is established. That clawback would also apply where a policy is cancelled during its free-look period and commission has already been paid out.

Just Rights for Children Alliance (JRCA) is currently at the center of a significant Supreme Court of India hearing regarding minors’ access to social media.  In a hearing on September 28, 2026, a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V Mohana directed the Central Government to frame statutory rules enforcing an 18-year age limit for social media accounts. 

Key developments include:
** Void Contracts: The Court highlighted that under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, minors are incompetent to contract, making their acceptance of social media terms of service legally void.

** Government Action: The Solicitor General confirmed the government plans to amend the IT Intermediary Rules to prevent platforms from allowing users under 18 to create accounts, potentially requiring parental consent or strict age verification.

** Platform Liability: The Court warned that social media intermediaries could lose safe harbor protection under Section 79 of the IT Act if they fail to implement effective safeguards against online grooming, sexual exploitation, and cyberbullying.

** Next Steps: The matter is listed for further hearing in four weeks as the government formulates the new regulatory framework.

     This follows JRCA’s earlier landmark success in September 2024 (Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish), where the Supreme Court ruled that the mere possession and storage of child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) is a punishable offense under the POCSO Act.

#BREAKING In what the Bench confirmed is the first ruling by any Supreme Court on the issue, the Supreme Court of India holds that a valid contractual notice is sufficient to terminate a bareboat charter. Physical repossession or redelivery of the vessel is not a precondition for termination.

The Court holds that after termination, the former charterer’s continuing possession is only as a gratuitous bailee. A maritime creditor cannot arrest the vessel for that entity’s liabilities if it was no longer the demise charterer when the arrest was effected.

The Court allows the appeal and sets aside the arrest of MV Nereus Progress, finding that its charter stood terminated on November 13, 2025, before its arrest on December 4.

When counsel said this was the first judgment by any Supreme Court on the subject, CJI Surya Kant said: “We have distinguished the Hong Kong and Singapore judgments also in our judgment. And yes, indeed.”

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Can the Government suspend a political party’s Instagram handle without a clear statutory power? And can a politician boycott a courtroom while simultaneously asking the Supreme Court to transfer the same judge from hearing his case?  

This week, the Aam Aadmi Party raised both questions in two different constitutional courtrooms.  

In the Supreme Court, AAP challenged the suspension of its Gujarat unit’s Instagram handle, arguing that Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act was never meant to become a direct content-blocking weapon. 

Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat argued that the provision only deals with “safe harbour” obligations of intermediaries — not independent censorship powers.  The party says the move violates Article 19(1)(a), the constitutional guarantee of free speech. 

The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the Centre.  At the same time in the Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma appointed three amicus curiae for Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, and Satyendar Jain after the leaders chose to boycott proceedings, invoking “Mahatma Gandhi’s Satyagraha principles” and claiming their faith in the court process had been shaken.  

But here’s the constitutional twist: Kejriwal had also moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the excise policy case away from Justice Sharma’s bench — even as his legal team withdrew from participation before her court.  

This has now created a rare constitutional confrontation involving: 
⚖️ Article 19 vs state regulation of digital speech 
⚖️ Article 21 vs procedural fairness in criminal prosecution 
⚖️ Judicial recusal vs courtroom boycott 
⚖️ Free speech, due process, and strategic constitutional litigation  Justice Sharma’s response may become one of the most significant procedural moments in the case: instead of proceeding ex parte, she chose to appoint independent senior advocates as amicus curiae to preserve procedural fairness.  

And one line from the Supreme Court hearing may define this entire battle: “Today my portal is gone.”  Because this is no longer just about an Instagram account.

 It is about whether opposition parties in India can lose their digital voice overnight — and what constitutional remedy exists when that happens.

The Union Government and Delhi Police have told Delhi High Court X is liable to lose its safe harbour protection in India because it failed to act against Rana Ayyub’s offensive tweets about Hindu deities and Savarkar.

Here’s @barandbench report on what transpired in court:

The Government has said that the police had issued notices in September 2025 and December 2025, requesting X to take down Ayyub’s posts. The Government said that in January 2025, a trial court ordered registration of an FIR against Ayyub over these posts.

The police notices and trial court order constitute “actual knowledge” under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, triggering a statutory obligation on X to act expeditiously and remove such unlawful content, the High Court has been told.

It added that as X failed to act despite “actual knowledge” the safe harbour protection available to it is liable to be withdrawn.

Notably, the High Court had on April 8, 2026 observed that these tweets (made between 2013-2017) were derogatory and communal. 

After the hearing, the Delhi Police sent a request to MEITY to block the content and the request is under consideration, the Court has been told.

Meanwhile, X has also filed a response in the High Court and said that the petition should be directed against Rana Ayyub (the uploader of the content) and not X. 

It also also directions to Delhi Police to follow the  2009 Blocking Rules and issue a blocking order under Section 69A of the IT Act.

Rana Ayyub's lawyers told the Court today that the writ petition was not maintainable. 

The HC has granted Ayyub two weeks time to file a reply in the case, including on the issue of maintainability.

In the weeks before he sued, a fake version of Anil Kapoor was making the rounds online. Not a lookalike, not an impersonator hired for a wedding gig, but a synthetic one. Generative AI tools had lifted the veteran actor’s face and stitched it onto other actors’ bodies and animated characters. His voice, pulled from decades of film dialogue, had been cloned into ringtones and GIFs. A website was charging people money for “motivational” advice supposedly delivered by Kapoor himself. Elsewhere, someone was selling mugs, t-shirts, and stickers stamped with his image and his signature catchphrase, “Jhakaas,” as if he’d personally signed off on the merchandise line. Dozens of domain names carrying his name had been quietly registered by people who had never met him.

Kapoor had no time for the usual legal process. Indian law generally requires parties to attempt mediation before filing a commercial suit, and defendants are normally heard before a court grants relief. But the infringers were anonymous, scattered, and multiplying by the day: the kind of problem where waiting for procedure to run its course means the harm is already irreversible by the time the case is heard. So Kapoor’s lawyers asked the Delhi High Court to skip ahead, granting an emergency injunction before the other side even showed up, under Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure, against Simply Life India and twenty other defendants, among them e-commerce sellers, a GIF platform, three domain registrars, and an unidentified class of “John Doe” infringers still to be discovered.

By Sarvagya Chaturvedi 

https://t.co/Kfzhg4STpt

On 20 September 2023, Justice Pratibha M. Singh gave them exactly that, and in doing so handed down what is now the founding order in an entirely new category of Indian law, built with no legislation behind it at all. This order didn’t invent personality rights in India. It didn’t need to. Indian courts have recognised for decades that a person’s identity (how they look, sound, and are recognised) has value, and that value belongs to them. In R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (1994), the Supreme Court grounded a right to control one’s own persona in the right to privacy under Article 21 of the Constitution. In Titan Industries v. Ramkumar Jewellers (2012), the Delhi High Court built on that foundation with a workable test: does the plaintiff hold an enforceable right in their own identity, is that identity recognisable from the defendant’s use, and, the sharper point, does establishing that require any proof that consumers were actually confused or deceived? Titan’s answer was no: identifiability alone does the work. Trademark or copyright registration not required.

What made the Kapoor case different wasn’t the doctrine. It was the technology it was applied to. This was the first time an Indian court had to decide whether the Titan framework, designed for stolen photographs and unauthorised endorsements, could stretch to cover something that didn’t exist when the test was written: a synthetically generated version of a person that had never actually said or done the things it appeared to.

https://t.co/Kfzhg4Trf1

Justice Singh’s answer was that it could, and then some. Her order restrained the sixteen defendants found to be actively infringing from using Kapoor’s face, voice, signature, or catchphrase in any unauthorised commercial context (morphed images, AI-cloned voice, merchandise, the lot) and went further, restraining “other unknown persons” from disseminating the specific pornographic and defamatory videos listed on a 44-link annexure to the order, with domain registrars ordered to lock three squatted domains and internet service providers ordered to take the listed links down immediately. It is not, on its face, an order against the world: it names defendants and it names links. 

But it is written to grow. New infringing links can be added to the annexure without Kapoor having to file a fresh suit each time, which functions, in practice, as something close to standing relief against anyone who does this next. And critically, the order accepted the logic underneath Kapoor’s petition, imported straight from Titan: the harm here doesn’t depend on whether a consumer was fooled into thinking Kapoor endorsed the product. The appropriation of his identity is itself the wrong, independent of confusion. That is a meaningfully aggressive reading of publicity rights, and it is the reading that generative AI has made necessary.

A deepfake doesn’t need to trick anyone into believing it’s real to still be a theft of someone’s likeness for profit.

🚨 #NewsAlert | The Delhi High Court has directed Meta Platforms to remove the morphed image of a woman shown with Prime Minister Narendra Modi from social media. The court issued notices to four CJP leaders named by the woman and directed Delhi Police to provide her protection following her claim of receiving life threats. The matter will be heard next on October 14.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

A Possible Explanation:

The US knew there was a threat to RAF Fairford - that's not in dispute here. The FPCON changes, armed patrol vehicles inside the base and concrete barricades all show that.

It seems possible to me that perhaps these 5 lads (or 8-10 if the eyewitness farmer is correct) were not actually there to attack the base - perhaps (given the fake fuel vans) they were actually in the area trying to steal fuel from local vehicles.

The farmer sees it, calls police. Police (who likely were aware of the USAF concerns) swarm into the area having perhaps not expected the "attackers" so soon. They manage to arrest 5 suspects and treat the 3 vans with every necessary precaution (as they should) - evacuating the neighbourhood, bringing Army EOD in, etc.

The males are initially arrested for Explosives Act offences (pending a safe way to check inside the vans) & go to custody. In the circumstances, further arrested for the Terrorism Act offence. However, after seizing whatever evidence they could (and examining the vans), it looks like police may have determined these aren't the attackers - as I say, potentially fuel thieves in the wrong place at the wrong time?

It's worth noting that if the terrorism act offences were looking likely, police could keep them detained for 48hrs initially before requiring a court to approve a longer period of time. Alternatively under normal arrest powers contained within the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, they can be held for 24hrs initially (extended to 36hrs under authority of a Police Superintendent if specific requirements are met), and up to 72hrs if a further extension is authorised by a court. Now clearly if they were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning and conveyed either to a local custody, or a dedicated counter-terrorism custody (likely closest in London), the fact they've been bailed today suggests they've spent at most 24-30hrs in custody before evidential review officers and the Crown Prosecution Service have determined there is insufficient evidence to charge them with an offence right now.

So they bail them with conditions not to contact each other as is normal procedure for vehicle interference/theft offences like that. But police need to download and analyse phones, and anything potentially seized from home addresses in order to ensure no link to the Iranian government or IRGC.

Meanwhile, did the actual planned attack get foiled inadvertently? Perhaps? Trump told the world that the US had been monitoring the "attackers" for some time - I'd suggest that if these lads genuinely were just in the wrong place at the wrong time, the actual suspects are now staying hidden until this all blows over a bit.

Either way, we don't have all the facts and that's part of any criminal or CT investigation - so yes, it sounds bad and arguably CTP could have done a better job of explaining it to the public, but they have to play their cards close to their chest right now in case my guesswork here is right and the suspects are still out there somewhere.

Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar held a press conference today and said it straight.

Bro, you vote every five years. 
You stand in the sun for an hour. 
And one day some stranger fills a form saying "this man doesn't live here" and your name is gone. 
You find out at the booth, when it is too late. 😡

This is what the SIR has become. 
The Election Commission should be protecting your vote. 
Instead it is the one that has to be forced to even order an inquiry.

Gyanesh Kumar, answer one thing. 
Who is going to be punished for this? 
Modi ji, your workers or no workers, the vote is still being cut. 🔥🔥

No Software for Hard Country

The EVM has ruined the Indian election. India taught the world the joy of delayed gratification. Intezaar ka phal meetha hota hai. But what we get is the pungent that is instant.

Two months of rallies, rath yatras, roadshows and revdi ruckus, and the result is out before lunch. Itni zaldi chai bhi thandi nahi hoti. You sit through a 60-day season and the finale is over in two minutes. Maggi takes more time, Gyanesh ji.

That is why the India Alliance’s demand for paper ballots makes sense. Press it hard, Indi men and women. For you, this is about trust. For the rest of us, this is about content. We long for a longer climax. 

Counting days were the only days this democracy was actually watchable. Leads swung like Test cricket on day five. A candidate trailing by 40,000 would be 12,000 ahead after the Ward 7 box opened, and the losing side would discover the word "recount". Now the machine says 2.3 lakh and the story is over. Where is the cliffhanger? Where is Badku Cha who sits outside the counting centre for 72 hours with one thermos and three  theories and more?

Software is for soft countries. India is a hard country. We want hardware. If we are doing elections, let us do it properly, and revive the democracy and old-style allegations too. A democracy that goes paperless has no paper trail to pin it all on Gyanu. The EVM can be accused only of being hacked, which is very lazy and technical. Compare that with the golden age.

Booth capturing, a genuine skill, began as early as 1957. Begusarai, I love you. It needed planning, manpower, lathis (guns were not available easily then) and a sense of timing. It was labour intensive, employment generating and, a Make in India initiative. The booth looter had to walk to the school building in June and scare voters away. Not like some geek like Saurabh Bhardwaj cracking the code open for all, except the Election Commission, to see.

People who have seen the good old days would remember ballot stuffing. That was the our crowdfunding. 100% polling to save democracy. We, including children, had to fold all those ballots. They did not have craftsmanship. But they did not cheat. They had to be multiple stampers. One man, one vote was the theory. One man, 40 votes was the practice. The wrist would tire and the pad of ink would go dry. Stamp duty. Today's voter presses a button and the machine goes beep, like a microwave. The old voter put his whole shoulder into it. Dignity of labour, thy name was chhaapo. Reclaim it.

There were the great moments of the invalid vote. A mohar placed with confidence in the centre of the rectangle, crossing the line, kissing the border, or landing on two symbols was generally not indecision or bipartisanship but just clumsy. Thousands of ballots were rejected for this. What a pity!

No machine will ever give you the thrill of a returning officer holding a ballot up to the light, with 10 agents arguing whether the smudge is a symbol or dried booger.

Add to this the missing keys, the boxes that went to the wrong godown, the polling agent who slept through the whole thing, and the unforgettable counting hall where there will be a power cut at the exact moment of the lead change. Pure cinema.

Some would say that paper ballots are slower, messier and more open to mischief. Loser talk. If paper ballots is complicated, so is a Test series. So is love. We are a cricket loving nation. Test cricket is real cricket. This T20 novelty will run out and our love for Tests will endure. Bring back Test cricket.

Let democracy take its time. Let the results come on the fourth or fifth day, after a recount, a stay order and a Baghpat style battle outside the strong room. Let us make some sacrifices for our democracy, as our forefathers did.

Democracy at a press of the button is no fun. Bring back the ballot. Stamp it and stuff it like we used to. Long live India. Long live Indian democracy. Jai Hind. Bharat Mata Ki Jai. Gyanu must go.

Global: This afternoon Starlink experienced another global outage, with services being down for all users around the world for about 15 minutes. This marks the second time this month that a major outage of the Starlink system has been reported. No cause for the outage has been provided.
