Maryland: This afternoon a large explosion was reported onboard a cargo vessel that was transiting outbound from Baltimore, bound for Mauritius. The M/V *W SAPPHIRE* experienced an explosion in one of her forward cargo holds shortly after leaving port. Her current position remains east of Bodkin Creek, and multiple tugboats and firefighting vessels remain on scene to keep her under control.

Analyst Comment: As this is a developing situation, there's no further information on what caused the blast, or the fate of the crew.

Washington D.C. - This afternoon President Zelenskyy returned to the White House, continuing diplomatic efforts to achieve peace in Ukraine.

Analyst Comment: Regarding the potential for peace, the situation remains tenuous. Following the negotiations with Putin on Friday, Russia's position appears to be largely the same as when the war started; Russia wants the Donetsk and also the "freezing" of front lines where they are right now on all fronts. Ukraine's position is equally hardline, with Zelenskyy also reiterating Ukraine's position of ceding zero terrain in any prospective peace deal.

Utah: A shooting was reported at a residence in Tremonton yesterday evening, which resulted in two police officers being killed, and one other wounded. Officers initially responded to this address due to multiple 911 hangups, and upon arrival, a barricaded shooter engaged them from within the house.

Analyst Comment: What led to this shooting is unclear, but 911 hangups are frequently utilized by individuals seeking to take their own life by the actions of the police, or by those seeking to ambush authorities. In this case, the latter seems to have been the result, which turned into a protracted small arms engagement. Multiple pre-made incendiary devices were recovered from the residence after the shooting, indicating that this was a planned ambush of some kind.

Florida: Vehicular homicide charges have been filed against Harjinder Singh for his role in the death of three people on the Florida Turnpike last week. Singh was attempting to conduct an illegal u-turn on the interstate, which resulted in him positioning his semi truck completely perpendicular to the road, completely blocking all lanes of traffic. Three people traveling in a minivan were unable to stop in time, colliding with the semi's trailer, resulting in their deaths.

-----END TEARLINE-----

Analyst Comment: The case involving the crash in Florida has gained nationwide notoriety for two main reasons. Firstly, the in-cabin video showing the crash was published immediately, which not only shows the exceptionally graphic nature of the crash, but also the lack of any sort of remorse from the driver after the crash. The social reaction to this video has resulted in more focus on this case, which leads to the second reason for the attention...this case gets worse the more one digs for details.

After the accident, Singh was revealed to have been an illegal immigrant from India, who crossed over the southern US border in 2018. Singh was allowed to get a driver's license in California (as this state allows illegals to get a license through the AB 60 program). From there, he was able to get his CDL license in the same state, despite federal law banning illegals from obtaining CDLs.

As a reminder, Singh was already in the United States illegally, so he's already a criminal right up front. This might not seem to be important, but when he arrived in 2018 H1B visas were being handed out like candy. Anyone in India had free reign to come to the United States, *especially* when it comes to industries like the trucking industry. This begs the question: If it was (and still is) so incredibly easy for Indians to come to the United States legally...why did Singh go through the hassle (and the danger) of sneaking under the fence illegally? Right now it's just hunch, but there may be other reasons as to why Mr. Singh did not want his name run through federal databases upon entry into the United States.

More importantly than the criminal negligence of one illegal is realizing how systemic this problem is. Singh was not joyriding around...he was working for a company which has a name, business license, and mailing address: White Hawk Carriers. While Singh himself has been arrested and charged...no one at this company has been arrested for allowing an illegal immigrant to work for them in violation of labor laws. In fact, Florida's official statements regarding this crash made no mention of the company he was working for. Observers only found out which company it was after reviewing the post-accident videos and seeing the logo (and the DoT number) painted on the door. When it comes to companies that sport a DOT identification number, a wealth of information is available online via several databases (such as the Safety Measurement System) which paint a clear picture. For instance, out of the 68x times this company's trucks were inspected on the highway in 2023, 36x of those inspections resulted in violations. So far this year this company has been cited for 19x Hours of Service violations.

As if that was not serious enough, a closer look at the company's ownership is even more illuminating. White Hawk Carriers Inc. is a company registered in California. The Secretary of State's database confirms this company is run by one Navneet Kaur.

The initial investigation points to this person's name very likely being used for obfuscation. It's very common for shady businesses to be registered in a spouses name, or in the name of a family member if the person who's actually running the company has legal trouble, or is in the United States illegally. Running this name through the other businesses registered in the same name turns out a whole host of other companies ranging from tax preparation companies and dry cleaners...to other trucking companies. The initial partial list of which is as follows:

- Navn Transport (Stockton, CA)
- Gobind Trucking (Lathrop, CA)
- Naav Enterprises (Menteca, CA)
- America One Logistics Company (Tracy, CA)
- American Auto and E Solutions (Lathrop, CA)

This list is incomplete as when searching the databases for associates of these companies, the links to other businesses are nearly endless. Each of these companies is registered to a different mailing address, and when each of those addresses is cross-referenced to find other businesses using that same address, potentially tens of thousands of "businesses" are linked together in some way, either by owner name or mailing address.

Most disturbingly, Kaur (or whoever is actually running the companies) appears to be engaging in the timeless tradition of simply changing business names when one of their trucking companies is banned from the road. For instance, there are around half a dozen trucking company LLC's that Kaur had previously registered in California. When cross-referenced with the DoT's safety databases, the picture becomes more clear. Whenever one trucking company gets too many violations and eventually gets banned from operating in the United States, they simply fold that LLC up, register a new one, and transfer the employees and trucks to the new LLC name. Various permitting hoops are jumped through and a new DoT identification number is issued for the new carrier...meaning that the same exact people get a fresh start with zero repercussions for previous safety violations.

In this case, Kaur registered a suspiciously similar company by the name of White Star Transport Inc, which had it's operating authority involuntarily revoked in 2015. Almost immediately after White Star Transport Inc folded, White Hawk Carriers Inc (the company involved in the crash) was registered and granted authority to operate within the United States. On Tuesday, the day of the fatal crash, the insurance policy for White Hawk Carriers was canceled. This could mean that the cycle will very likely continue as this LLC is rolled up and a new company created when the situation cools down.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Customers are blamed.

text:
The facts behind Hal von Luebbert v. City of Lubbock, Steven Greene, Taylor Ruggles, and Dr. Breanna Harris are very simple to understand and assess. The City of Lubbock and these people treated two of their fellow citizens like antebellum slaves, with no civil rights of any kind. Worse, Deputy City Attorney Jeff Hartsell said in an official statement, "We don't think we did anything wrong."

What WAS it that they did? While contemptuously ignoring both the rule of law and every civil right of a U.S. citizen, they seized and destroyed my dog. In the process they also ignored my challenge to the Municipal Court's jurisdiction, a challenge that same court validated and conceded only a few days later, after my dog had been killed.

On the basis of a totally uninvestigated and unverified report by a woman who, in her own sworn affidavit and self-styled "action plan," admitted running from behind at a leashed and sitting dog, THEY KILLED MY DOG ILLEGALLY. Period.

Is that all? Hardly.

August 30, Melrose Park: An Irish Setter attacked Max and me. I broke two bones in my hand. The officer who arrived left me collapsed against my car without a word. I have asked the City eight times, in writing, who owned the dog and whether it had rabies. No answer, in more than a year.

September 14, Leftwich Park: Two Siberian Huskies attacked us. Rita used pepper spray and I fired a shot in the air. The police ignored the dogs, verbally attacked me, and took my pistol. I have never gotten it back. The City won't identify the officers.

September 15, the Animal Services "hearing": Hard of hearing, I heard almost nothing; the bailiff threatened to remove me each time I asked. No one was sworn in. I was denied rulings on my motions in limine because the clerk of court had thrown them all away. I was permitted no cross-examination. I gave notice of appeal while still in the room and mailed it that afternoon.

September 16: Rita went to Animal Services in my place, to comply and bring Max home. She was handed a letter falsely claiming homeowners insurance didn't cover dog bites, a letter the City's own database shows was prepared before she arrived. Under threats about Max's fate, she signed.

September 17: Little Max was killed, although by law my appeal barred them from touching him for ten days.

September 30: The Municipal Court conceded it never had jurisdiction and called the matter "moot."

October to December: I sued. The County Clerk again took my lawsuit and filings and never filed them, wrote that she had "no record" of my case, and "forwarded" my papers to the City of Lubbock, the defendant. My case was opened only after a higher court forced it. That same December 2, the City enacted a new dangerous-dog ordinance, the first in seventeen years.

Since then: In more than a year, the City and its lawyers have not answered a single question. They tell the court my suit wasn't filed until the day the clerk let it in, that my questions came too early to answer, and now, under a stay, that my subpoenas are invalid.

BEFORE GOING FURTHER, however, I need to say what my purpose is in writing this. Yes, it's to make sure, as far as possible, that what happened to my wife and me never happens to anyone again. Yes, it is to see those who perpetrated this outrage held to account. BUT NONE OF THAT WILL HAPPEN UNLESS YOU, THE READER, AND AS MANY PEOPLE AS POSSIBLE, CHECK AND VERIFY EVERYTHING I SAY HERE. My purpose is to persuade as many people as I can to call the Lubbock City Attorney, City Council members Dr. Jennifer Wilson, Tim Green, Tim Collins, Gordon Harris, Christy Martinez-Garcia, and David Bruegel, and Mayor Mark McBrayer, and ask what's going on. I also want you to call the Lubbock news media responsible for the total blackout of information about my lawsuit and my circumstances.

Learn what the City of Lubbock, its City Attorney, and its news media are hiding.

DO NOT TAKE MY WORD FOR ANYTHING, not a syllable.

I’ve said what you will find. TRY me. What you will find that concerns you (you have no real interest in my troubles otherwise, and I don't ask you to) is this: when a city, its city attorney, its city council, and its court can do what was done and is still being done in Hal von Luebbert v. City of Lubbock, Steven Greene, Taylor Ruggles, and Texas Tech University Professor Dr. Breanna Harris, it can be done to you, and to some of you, it WILL be done.

Think about it. That's all I ask.

For the continuing record,
Hal von Luebbert

text:
Before action was taken to demolish parts of the Shahi Mosque in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, for road widening, the city’s Qazi and mosque officials reportedly asked local residents to leave the area at night by simply saying, “Go back to your homes.” However, they did not clearly inform them that parts of the mosque would be demolished in the morning.

Ujjain/Bhopal:
Tensions had been prevailing in Ujjain since Sunday night over the plan to remove a portion of the Shahi Mosque as part of an ongoing road-widening project being carried out in preparation for the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2028. Mosque committee members and religious leaders asked the people who had gathered during the night to return to their homes. However, many people alleged that they were not told that the demolition of part of the mosque would begin the following morning.
By morning, a large number of security personnel had been deployed at the site along with the administrative team and police force, and barricades were erected around the mosque. During this time, clashes between some protesters and the police were reported, including allegations of stone-pelting and the use of tear gas.
The administration says that the action to remove the portion of the mosque falling along the proposed route of the widened road is being carried out only after an order from the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The High Court had earlier dismissed two petitions, stating that the municipal corporation had followed due legal procedure.
Meanwhile, a large section of the local Muslim community said that they had merely been told to “go home” during the night, without being given details about the demolition schedule or the broader plan. As a result, many people remained near the mosque until morning, while some even spent the night inside it.

text:
The call came during second period. Calm, but with an edge. "Can you come down to Room 12? One of the eighth graders is refusing to remove his cap." 

When I got to my office, there he was. Jaden. Usually soft-spoken, respectful. But today he sat curled in the chair like he wanted to vanish. Cap pulled low. He muttered so quietly I almost missed it: "They laughed at me."

He told me kids in the cafeteria had made fun of his botched haircut. He slowly lifted his cap. His hair was butchered, lines jagged, and bald patches.

I stood and walked over to my cabinet and pulled out my old barber kit. Before I became a principal, I cut hair to pay for college. "Let me help, yeah?" I asked.

He nodded. I draped a towel over his shoulders and started shaping him up. 

As the first smooth line buzzed into place, he exhaled like someone finally let him breathe again. 

As I adjusted the angle for a final fade, I noticed something. Scars. Tiny, raised lines etched into the back of his scalp. I froze for half a second. "These... from something recent?" I asked softly.

He didn't answer right away. Then he whispered:
"That's where they hit me. Last year. When we were still at our old place." I turned the clippers off. "Who's 'they'?" I asked.

He didn't look at me. And then he said something that made my blood run cold "My mom's ex-boyfriend," he whispered, his voice so small it was almost swallowed by the quiet hum of the office. "He... he used to get mad. At her. At me. He'd throw things. The last time, it was a coffee mug." 

The clippers in my hand suddenly felt impossibly heavy. The botched haircut, the hat, the fear, it wasn't just about shame. It was about hiding. It was about survival.

"Jaden," I said, my voice steady despite the rage coiling in my gut. "Is he still around? Is your mom okay?"
He finally looked at me in the mirror, his eyes wide and haunted. "We left. A few months ago. We have a new apartment now. It's supposed to be better." 

He paused. "But he found us."
My blood ran cold. "When, Jaden?"
"Last night," he choked out, a single tear tracing a path through the tiny clipped hairs on his cheek. "He was waiting outside. He told my mom he was sorry.

He said he'd changed. She... she let him in." The haircut. It wasn't his cousin. It was him. A clumsy, cruel attempt at an apology, or worse, a mark of ownership.
I put the clippers down. The haircut was over. My real job was just beginning.

"Okay," I said, my voice leaving no room for argument. I put my hands on his shoulders, turning him to face me. "Here is what's going to happen. You are not going home on that bus today. You are going to stay right here with me. 

We're going to call your mom, and we're going to call some people who can help. People who make sure men like that go away and never come back. Do you understand?" He just nodded, a wave of relief so profound it seemed to uncurl his hunched shoulders.

For the next two hours, my office became a command center. I called Child Protective Services. I called the police. I spoke to Jaden's mother, who sobbed on the phone, admitting she was terrified but didn't know what to do.
When she arrived at the school, she wasn't alone. A police officer and a social worker were with her. They had a plan. An emergency protective order. A new place to go, a shelter with security, where he couldn't find them.
As Jaden got ready to leave with his mom, he stopped at my office door. His hair was perfect. But more than that, his eyes were clear. The fear was still there, but it wasn't hiding anymore.
"Thank you," he whispered.

"You're a good kid, Jaden," I said, my voice thick.
"You deserve to feel safe."

He reached up and touched the back of his head, where the scars were now hidden beneath the clean lines of his new haircut. "You know," he said, a small, hesitant smile on his face. "You're a pretty good barber."

This is a fictional story posted on Pinterest by Cecie Jay.

#DemsUnited

text:
Caleb would receive a generous trust allowance and could inherit voting shares after my death, provided he met specific conditions.

He had to remain free of felony convictions.

He could not commit financial fraud against the estate.

He could not threaten, exploit, or assault me.

Most importantly, the trust contained a protective clause allowing me to remove him permanently if his conduct endangered the family or company.

Caleb did not know the exact language.

Henry insisted we keep it private.

“If he knows where the line is,” Henry told me, “he’ll learn to stand one inch away from it.”

Then he handed me a sealed letter.

Inside was one sentence I never forgot.

Protect what we built, even from our own son.

After Henry died, grief weakened every boundary I had.

Caleb called constantly.

He said losing his father had destroyed him.

He needed help stabilizing his life.

The first request was for eighty thousand dollars to repair a bad investment.

The second was for a replacement sports car after he crashed the one Henry had given him.

The third was a casino debt concealed behind the word business.

Each time, I paid.

Each time, Caleb cried, apologized, and promised it would never happen again.

Each rescue taught him the wrong lesson.

He did not learn that gambling was dangerous.

He learned that his mother would absorb the consequences.

This time, he had used my name as collateral.

This time, strangers had come to my home with photographs.

This time, I finally said no.

Caleb stared at me from the staircase.

“You have the money.”

“That does not make the debt mine.”

“They’re dangerous.”

“You knew that when you borrowed from them.”

His voice rose.

“I’m your son!”

“And I am your mother, not your private bank.”

He descended one step at a time.

“You would let them hurt me?”

“I will pay for treatment. I will pay for a legitimate attorney. I will help you enter a gambling-recovery program.”

“I don’t need treatment.”

“You owe nearly half a million dollars to criminals.”

“I need a check.”

“You are not getting one.”

His smile vanished.

Then his hand hit my shoulder.

The fall was fast, bright, and nearly silent.

I struck the marble and lost my breath.

Caleb came down slowly.

He crouched beside me, close enough that I could see the small scar above his eyebrow from when he fell off his bicycle at seven.

I had held a towel against that wound while he cried into my chest.

Now his face contained no trace of that child.

“Tomorrow, you’ll call the bank,” he whispered. “Or next time, I won’t miss.”

Then he took my phone from the side table, deleted the message containing the photographs, and walked out.

He made one mistake.

He forgot the camera.

Five years earlier, after my hip surgery, Henry installed a discreet security camera inside the staircase alcove.

It monitored the stairs in case I fell while alone.

The camera automatically uploaded footage to a protected server controlled by the estate security company.

Caleb believed the system had been disconnected after Henry’s death.

It had not.

I remained on the floor for almost ten minutes.

When I finally stood, my ribs ached and my left arm felt heavy.

At midnight, I sat in Henry’s study with an ice pack pressed against my side.

His desk still carried faint scratches from the years he used it.

His reading glasses remained inside the top drawer because I could never bring myself to move them….

text:
I called Dr. Samuel Levin, our family physician.

He came to the house, examined my shoulder and ribs, documented the bruising, and insisted I go for imaging the following morning.

Then I called Jonathan Graves, Henry’s estate attorney.

“Mrs. Whitmore?” he answered, his voice thick with sleep.

“Jonathan, I need you to come tomorrow.”

Something in my tone woke him completely.

“Are you safe?”

I looked toward the empty staircase.

“Safe enough.”

“What happened?”

“Caleb crossed the line.”

There was a pause.

“Which line?”

“All of them.”

I explained the gambling debt, the forged collateral, the blow, and the threat.

Jonathan’s voice became sharp.

“Call the police.”

“I will.”

“Tonight.”

“The security company has the recording. Dr. Levin documented the injuries. I need tomorrow handled carefully.”

“What do you need from me?”

“Bring witnesses. Bring a notary. Bring the documents Henry and I discussed five years ago.”

Another silence.

Then he asked, “It’s time?”

I closed my eyes.

“Yes.”

The next morning, I went to the hospital for X-rays.

Nothing was broken, but my shoulder was badly bruised and two ribs were strained.

A police detective named Karen Doyle met me in a private room.

I gave a full statement.

The security company provided the staircase footage.

Detective Doyle watched it once, then asked whether Caleb had access to weapons.

I said he owned a licensed handgun, though I did not know where he kept it.

She advised me not to confront him alone.

“I won’t be alone,” I said.

Jonathan arrived at noon with two other attorneys.

Martin Bell specialized in corporate governance.

Elijah Ross represented the family trust.

A licensed notary came with them.

They spread documents across Henry’s dining table.

The protective clause was stronger than I remembered.

If Caleb committed violence against me, misused the family name as collateral, threatened estate assets, or exposed Whitmore Logistics to criminal liability, I could remove him as a beneficiary immediately.

His trust income could be terminated.

His future shares could be redistributed.

His access to company property, vehicles, accounts, and residences could be revoked.

The only requirement was documented evidence and notarized confirmation from me.

We had both.

Jonathan looked at the bruise beneath my sleeve.

“You do not have to serve him dinner.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you doing this?”

“Because he expects me to surrender.”

“That sounds dangerous.”

“Detective Doyle will have officers nearby.”

Jonathan studied me.

“This isn’t revenge?”

“No.”

“What is it?”

I looked at Henry’s chair at the head of the table.

“The last consequence his father tried to prepare him for.”

By three that afternoon, the documents were signed.

Caleb was removed as beneficiary, voting heir, and successor to Whitmore Logistics.

His monthly trust payment was suspended.

The company canceled his executive consultant title, which had always been mostly ceremonial.

His corporate cards were frozen.

His access credentials were revoked.

The security team recovered the company-owned Range Rover from his apartment garage….

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

A woman employee at Tech Mahindra Dundigal campus, Hyderabad, says she was terminated after taking three days of leave to care for her sick 11 year old daughter.

She had reportedly joined the company only about four and a half months earlier.

She says she was asked to log in and wait for approval, but left after repeated calls from her daughter and informed the company that she would make up the work.

What happens to working mothers when family emergency becomes a workplace liability?

Companies can have targets, deadlines and attendance policies. But if a mother has to choose between her sick child and her job, what exactly are we calling family friendly or this entire charade of women back to workplace?

The couple had been arrested by the Rajasthan Police in the matter. While passing the order, the Supreme Court observed that criminal provisions cannot be used for the recovery of money.

Chief Justice of India Justice Suryakant also issued a notice to the Rajasthan government on their bail plea, directing the state to respond within a week.

The bench further directed that both be released immediately upon furnishing bail bonds. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for next Thursday.

text:
Somewhere in 1945, at the dead of the night, the British intelligence intercepted a suspicious-looking seagoing trawler near the coast of Mumbai. A team of police raided the trawler but could find only kitchen utensils and gunny bags. The trawler was travelling from Yangon in Myanmar and the cargo belonged to a Gujarati engineer, B. C. Mehta. As soon as the trawler reached the coast Mehta took all the bags and utensils with him and went straight to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

Why would a man coming from Yangon take those insignificant utensils and gunny bags to one of the tallest leaders of the Indian freedom struggle? 

Mehta was, in fact, on a very important mission. The mission was to tell the tales of bravery of valour displayed by Azad Hind Fauj on the battle field. Those gunny bags were hiding reels of a documentary film made by the propaganda unit of Fauj.

When Fauj led by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose started suffering reverses in the war it was felt that Indians living in India needed to know the real story of Netaji. The British government had put severe censors on any news of Azad Hind Fauj. Indians were fed with a narrative that Netaji was a Japanese agent and Fauj was nothing but the Indian Japanese Fighting Force formed to establish Japanese colonialism in India. Though Fauj had a propaganda unit, its penetration into the Indian mainland was not much.

The propaganda unit of Fauj on the orders of Netaji made a documentary film that showed Netaji, soldiers on the battlefield, Rani Jhansi regiment, and other engagements of Fauj. Netaji might have left India after bitter differences with Mahatma Gandhi but he still had his sympathizers and allies in the Indian National Congress. These pro-Netaji leaders were contacted so that the film could be shown to the Indian public.

Mehta was a Gujarati engineer belonging to a business family who would, several times, drive Netaji in his vehicle in Myanmar. Sardar Patel was contacted by Azad Hind Fauj regarding this film. He pledged his support to smuggle the film into India and Mehta was given the responsibility to bring it into Indian territory.

Sardar Patel took the reels of the film with him and rushed to New Delhi. The film needed to be watched by all the senior Congress leaders. Patel asked Congress activists to arrange for a public screening of the film. Rajeshwar Dayal, owner of Regal Cinema at Connaught Place, was requested to allow screening at his theatre. He agreed and screening was arranged.

On the scheduled day Sardar Patel, Jawahar Lal Nehru, Maulana Azad, and each of the members of the Congress High Command watched the film. The outlook towards Azad Hind Fauj and Netaji was changed. People realized that Netaji was on a national mission to free his motherland and evil propaganda of the British that he was a Japanese agent was a lie. Gautam Kaul writes, “The film showed sequences of the members of Azad Hind Fauj training in the jungle and also the work of Rani of Jhansi Brigade of Indian women based in Yangon and Singapore. It also featured Bose moving around on inspection and meeting with other leaders of the region as well as exhorting his workers to prepare themselves for a long march to Delhi.”

After the screening, as expected, Dayal received a notice from the government for violating the law. Rajinder Narain, who also argued at the famous Red Fort INA trials, was asked by Dayal to help him. Narain took him to Kunwar Mohinder Singh Bedi, who was the city magistrate then, and asked for his help. Bedi knew how to help a patriot within the ambit of colonial law. After the first hearing, he declared a long vacation. He did not list the case for hearings until India got independence.

X has received executive orders from the Indian government requiring X to block over 8,000 accounts in India, subject to potential penalties including significant fines and imprisonment of the company’s local employees. The orders include demands to block access in India to accounts belonging to international news organizations and prominent X users.

In most cases, the Indian government has not specified which posts from an account have violated India's local laws. For a significant number of accounts, we did not receive any evidence or justification to block the accounts.

To comply with the orders, we will withhold the specified accounts in India alone. We have begun that process. However, we disagree with the Indian government’s demands. Blocking entire accounts is not only unnecessary, it amounts to censorship of existing and future content, and is contrary to the fundamental right of free speech.

This is not an easy decision, however keeping the platform accessible in India is vital to Indians’ ability to access information.

We believe that making these executive orders public is essential for transparency – lack of disclosure discourages accountability and can contribute to arbitrary decision making. However, due to legal restrictions, we are unable to publish the executive orders at this time.

X is exploring all possible legal avenues available to the company. Unlike users located in India, X is restricted by Indian law in its ability to bring legal challenges against these executive orders. However, we encourage all users who are impacted by these blocking orders to seek appropriate relief from the courts.

Users may contact any of the below legal aid organizations:
iProbono India (https://t.co/HnfseKQ2Lb)
National Legal Services Authority (https://t.co/fYOZjp2MZA)
Karnataka Legal Services Authority (https://t.co/Plh3c9p9wP)
Supreme Court Legal Services (https://t.co/Sazj55Co08)

We have provided the affected users with notice of the actions in accordance with our policies. Affected users may also contact the Indian government at cyberlaw@meity.gov.in.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal. Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.
